note: Every prompt in this file was written for this companion. Nothing here is a quotation from a saint, a father, a hymn, or a liturgical text, and nothing should be presented as one. Prompts are questions and small intentions in the app's own voice, selected deterministically by date so a given day always shows the same prompt. The August 1-15 overlay always takes precedence over these pools.
label: A prompt from this companion — not a liturgical text.

selection.explanation: For each day: if the Dormition overlay has content, use it. Otherwise try a rank pool (pascha, great-feast, forefeast, apodosis, sunday), then a cycle pool (triodion, great-lent, holy-week, bright-week, pentecostarion), then a fasting-season pool (nativity-fast, apostles-fast), then the Wednesday/Friday pool on those weekdays when the day is a fast day, then the ordinary pool.

pascha.focus: The feast of feasts. Everything the year has been for arrives today.
pascha.journal: Where were you at the moment the light came into the church — and what do you want to remember about it?
pascha.mercy: Invite someone to the table today who was not expecting to be invited.

great-feast.focus: A Great Feast of the Church. The ordinary week bends around it; let the household bend a little too.
great-feast.journal: What is this feast asking our family to see that a normal day hides?
great-feast.mercy: Mark the day for someone else — a call, a meal, a candle lit for them.

great-feast.focus: The Church keeps feasts with the body: standing, singing, eating, gathering. Keep this one with more than your thoughts.
great-feast.journal: If we could hold one image from today's services, what would it be?
great-feast.mercy: Share the feast's food with a neighbour or someone at the parish.

forefeast.focus: A forefeast — the Church leaning toward what is coming. Preparation is itself part of the celebration.
forefeast.journal: What would it look like for our house to be ready for this feast, practically and quietly?
forefeast.mercy: Do one act of preparation for someone else's feast, not your own.

forefeast.focus: The eve of a feast is for getting the house of the heart in order, not for hurry.
forefeast.journal: What needs setting down before tomorrow?
forefeast.mercy: Make peace with anyone in the household before the feast begins.

apodosis.focus: The leavetaking of a feast. The Church says goodbye slowly, so that the feast can settle in rather than vanish.
apodosis.journal: What did this feast leave with us, now that it is being set aside?
apodosis.mercy: Thank someone who made the feast possible — clergy, chanters, kitchen, drivers.

sunday.focus: Sunday is a small Pascha. Whatever the season, the Resurrection sets today's table.
sunday.journal: What did I notice in the Liturgy this morning that I had not noticed before?
sunday.mercy: Greet someone at church you have not yet spoken to.

sunday.focus: The week begins from the altar, not from Monday's list.
sunday.journal: What is one thing from today's Gospel to carry into the week?
sunday.mercy: Offer a ride, a meal, or an hour to someone in the parish.

sunday.focus: Rest is commanded, not merely permitted. Let some part of today be genuinely still.
sunday.journal: Where does our family actually rest — and is it restoring us?
sunday.mercy: Give someone in the house an hour off from their usual work.

triodion.focus: The Triodion has opened. The Church begins turning toward Great Lent weeks before it arrives, gently, one Sunday at a time.
triodion.journal: What is this year's Lent going to need from me that last year's did not?
triodion.mercy: Begin now: one small generosity that could become a Lenten habit.

triodion.focus: These pre-Lenten weeks ask for honesty before they ask for effort.
triodion.journal: Where am I still excusing something I already know needs to change?
triodion.mercy: Apologize for something small that you have been letting slide.

great-lent.focus: The Great Fast. Long enough that it cannot be performed — only lived, badly and then better.
great-lent.journal: Where is Christ inviting me to greater patience today?
great-lent.mercy: Give quietly, so that no one at home knows the amount.

great-lent.focus: Lent simplifies the table so that other things can grow: prayer, repentance, mercy. The food is the smallest part.
great-lent.journal: What unnecessary comfort can I release today, without judging anyone who does not?
great-lent.mercy: Listen to someone all the way through without preparing your reply.

great-lent.focus: The middle of a fast is where it stops being interesting. That is precisely where it starts to form us.
great-lent.journal: What have I learned about my own appetites since the fast began?
great-lent.mercy: Cook enough of something to give a portion away.

great-lent.focus: Prostrations, hunger, standing in long services — Lent is prayed with the body. Do what your body can, and let that be enough.
great-lent.journal: Where did I fail to love this week, and how can I begin again?
great-lent.mercy: Visit, call, or write to someone who is housebound or alone.

holy-week.focus: Holy Week. Clear the calendar of everything that can possibly move; nothing else this year is like these days.
holy-week.journal: Which service of this week do I most want our family to be present for, and what will it cost to be there?
holy-week.mercy: Take over someone's obligations so that they can be in church.

holy-week.focus: The Church walks to the Cross one day at a time. Do not skip ahead to Sunday.
holy-week.journal: What is hardest to look at in these days' services — and why?
holy-week.mercy: Forgive, concretely, one person you have been carrying a grievance against.

bright-week.focus: Bright Week — one day of Pascha stretched across seven. There is no fasting and no kneeling; there is only the feast.
bright-week.journal: What does it change to live a whole week as if it were Sunday?
bright-week.mercy: Bring paschal food or greetings to someone who could not be at the services.

pentecostarion.focus: The fifty days. The Church counts from Pascha the way a family counts from a birth.
pentecostarion.journal: What has this Pascha changed, now that some weeks have passed?
pentecostarion.mercy: Encourage someone whose Lent was hard.

nativity-fast.focus: The Nativity Fast — forty days walking toward the cave in Bethlehem while the world around us is already unwrapping.
nativity-fast.journal: How do we keep this season pointed at Christ in a household with lists, lights and deadlines?
nativity-fast.mercy: Set aside something each week of this fast for someone who will have a lean Christmas.

nativity-fast.focus: This fast is gentler than Lent but longer than it feels. Steadiness matters more than strictness.
nativity-fast.journal: What small daily practice could our family actually keep for forty days?
nativity-fast.mercy: Write to someone you have not thanked this year.

apostles-fast.focus: The Apostles' Fast — kept for the two who were made ready to give everything. Its length changes every year; its point does not.
apostles-fast.journal: What was I given that I have not yet handed on?
apostles-fast.mercy: Tell someone plainly what the faith has given you.

wedfri.focus: Wednesday and Friday are the week's two small fasts — one for the betrayal, one for the Cross. A quiet weekly rhythm older than any calendar on the wall.
wedfri.journal: What does this small regular fast do in a week that a long fast cannot?
wedfri.mercy: Skip one purchase today and pass the amount on.

wedfri.focus: A fast day inside an ordinary week. Nothing dramatic — just the table remembering.
wedfri.journal: Whom can I remember in prayer today?
wedfri.mercy: Do one household task that is not yours to do, and say nothing about it.

ordinary.focus: An ordinary day in the Church's year — which still has its saints, its readings, and its own quiet work.
ordinary.journal: What did I receive with gratitude today?
ordinary.mercy: Send a message to someone you have been meaning to check on.

ordinary.focus: Most of the Christian life is unremarkable days done faithfully.
ordinary.journal: What is one small thing done well today?
ordinary.mercy: Notice who is tired in this house, and lighten something for them.

ordinary.focus: The saints of today's calendar were mostly unknown in their own lifetimes. Obscurity is no obstacle.
ordinary.journal: Read today's saints' names slowly. Which one would you like to know more about?
ordinary.mercy: Pray for someone by name who will never know you did.
